content: Night terrors, also known as sleep terrors, are a type of sleep disorder where an individual abruptly awakens from sleep in a state of intense fear. Symptoms of Night Terrors: Children experiencing night terrors often scream and appear extremely frightened and confused. They may move violently and seem unaware of their surroundings. It is typically difficult to communicate with, comfort, or fully awaken a child during a night terror episode. Physical symptoms may include sweating, rapid breathing (hyperventilation), an accelerated heart rate (palpitations), and dilated pupils. These episodes usually last between 10 to 20 minutes, after which the child typically returns to sleep. Most children are unable to recall the event the following morning and often have no memory of the episode. Children with night terrors may also exhibit sleepwalking behaviors. Unlike night terrors, nightmares are more common in the early morning hours and are often triggered by watching frightening media or experiencing emotional stress. After a nightmare, individuals can usually recall the dream in detail and do not experience disorientation upon waking. Causes of Night Terrors: The exact cause of night terrors is unknown, but potential triggers include: Fever Sleep deprivation Periods of emotional tension, stress, or conflict Night terrors are most commonly observed in boys aged 5 to 7, though they can also occur in girls. They are relatively common in children aged 3 to 7 but become much less frequent as children grow older. There is evidence to suggest a familial predisposition to night terrors. While rare, night terrors can also occur in adults, particularly during times of emotional stress or with alcohol use. When to Seek Medical Attention: Consult a healthcare provider if: Night terrors occur frequently. They regularly disrupt sleep. Other symptoms accompany the night terrors. The episodes result in, or nearly result in, injuries. Diagnosis: In most cases, no additional testing or examination is required. If the night terrors are severe or prolonged, a psychological evaluation may be necessary. Treatment Options: In many cases, comforting the child during or after an episode is sufficient. Reducing stress or employing coping mechanisms may help decrease the frequency of night terrors. In some cases, talk therapy or counseling may be beneficial. Benzodiazepine medications, such as diazepam, taken at bedtime can reduce night terrors, but they are rarely used for this condition. Prognosis: Most children outgrow night terrors within a short period. The frequency of episodes typically decreases after the age of 10. It is rare for children to develop long-term difficulties with falling asleep or staying asleep as a result of night terrors. Prevention: Minimizing stress and utilizing effective coping strategies may help reduce the occurrence of night terrors. The number of episodes generally decreases as children grow older, particularly after the age of 10.
